Vignette:
Marcus, a 19-year-old African American man, first encountered the chilling reality of his world’s unpredictability a year ago, when a seemingly innocuous online connection spiralled into a terrifying ordeal of stalking. What began as a series of persistent messages on a gaming forum from an acquaintance escalated into unwanted presence, with the individual showing up uninvited at his apartment building, then his local coffee shop, and eventually making increasingly unsettling phone calls. Looking back, Marcus was certain the event happened because of the way he had acted. He replayed conversations, convinced that if he had been firmer, less polite, or simply ignored the initial messages, he could have prevented the whole terrifying situation. This self-blame became a constant companion, a quiet, accusatory voice in his mind.

After the stalking eventually ceased, leaving him physically unharmed but deeply scarred, Marcus found his perception of reality profoundly altered. He had come to believe that the world was a fundamentally dangerous place, a landscape of hidden threats lurking beneath the surface of everyday interactions. This conviction was not abstract; it manifested as a gnawing certainty that he had to be especially careful, because you never knew what could happen next. Every unexpected sound outside his apartment, every unfamiliar face in a crowd, every notification on his phone, became a potential harbinger of renewed danger.

As a UX designer, Marcus spent much of his time immersed in digital interfaces, crafting user-friendly experiences. His work, once a source of creative satisfaction, now often felt like a minefield. He worked remotely from his apartment, which initially felt like a safe haven, but even there, his vigilance never waned. He found himself constantly scanning the street outside his window, double-checking his security cameras, and frequently glancing at his phone, not for work, but to monitor incoming calls or messages, ready to block any unknown numbers. The collaborative nature of UX design, which often required video calls with clients or team members, became a source of intense anxiety. He dreaded meeting new people, even virtually, fearing that any interaction could open a door to another threat, another individual who might intrude upon his carefully constructed boundaries. He started declining opportunities to present his work in person, citing a preference for remote collaboration, but in truth, the thought of being in an unfamiliar environment, exposed and vulnerable, filled him with dread.

Over the past months, Marcus’s life had shrunk considerably. He stopped going to the local gym, cancelled plans with friends, and rarely left his apartment unless absolutely necessary. The once vibrant city outside his window, a place he used to explore with enthusiasm, now felt like a sprawling network of potential risks. His social life had dwindled to almost nothing, and his once-ambitious career trajectory had stalled. He found it increasingly difficult to focus on his design projects, the constant internal monitoring of his environment draining his mental energy. He often missed deadlines, not out of procrastination, but because the sheer exhaustion of perpetual vigilance made sustained concentration impossible. He knew this wasn't sustainable, that the isolation and the pervasive fear were slowly suffocating him. What frightened him most was the thought of living the rest of his life trapped in this state of constant alert, always waiting for the next unknown threat to emerge, never truly feeling safe. It was this overwhelming sense of entrapment, combined with a desperate longing to reclaim some semblance of his former life, that finally prompted Marcus to seek help.
